name: Dye fabric
blurb: Onion skins, avocado stones and black beans give real colour on wool and cotton. The chemistry matters more than the recipe: fibre type and mordant decide whether the colour lasts.
gear: Natural fibre fabric or yarn — dye will not take on polyester
A dedicated dye pot, never used for food again
Dye material: onion skins, avocado, madder, or a synthetic dye
steps: Scour the fabric first: wash it hot with detergent to remove finishes, or the dye will blotch.
Mordant the fibre with alum, which is what bonds the dye to the fibre and stops it washing out.
Make the dye bath by simmering your dye material, then strain out the solids.
Add the wet mordanted fabric and hold it below a simmer, stirring gently. Boiling wool will felt it.
Leave it in the cooling bath for hours or overnight for deeper colour.
Rinse until the water runs clear, and wash separately for the first few washes.
tips: Unmordanted natural dye is a stain, not a dye — it will fade within a few washes.
Keep dye equipment entirely separate from cookware, including mordants, which are not food safe.
Sudden temperature changes felt wool. Move it gently between baths of similar temperature.
proof: An evenly dyed piece that survives several washes without noticeable fading.
